chapter: Portraits from Hemphill to Getz, and the bebop question
title: Ben Webster from valet to Fletcher's band and 'Cottontail'
summary: Webster returned to Wilberforce with a tenor and joined Horace's band; Horace placed him with Vernon Andrade at the Renaissance and urged Fletcher to hire him. He played stride piano and wrote the 'Cottontail' reed chorus.

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong

blocks.x: Let's see. I'm trying to think of that nickname we used to call him. Ben had two or three. Ben was quite a guy. He had those big cueball eyes, and he could work them too, you know. And he always carried that big tone, and, of course, Coleman Hawkins was his idol, as far as playing. He carried that big tone with him all the time. And Ben Webster went to Wilberforce University. He wasn't one of the Collegians, as far as playing a horn was concerned, but he was our band valet, believe it or not. But that lasted only a year because we left school, it seems to me disintegrate during the summer, and, of course, everyone went their own way.
And we didn't see Ben the next year. It was about

a year later he came back to Wilberforce with a horn, tenor, and he could blow blew it. And he did join my band then, and we went to New York. And I first introduced him to Fletcher in his home, and he stayed there with us about a week or so, and I got Ben him a job in a ballroom there called the Renaissance Ballroom at 138th 150th and Seventh Avenue with a band that used to play for different clubs that would hire the band. It was a house band. named Vernond Andrades Androtti's. He was the leader there, and, of course, it was steady work because he would play five different affairs a week, you know, like banquets and all those things. I got Ben him a job there.
Of course, Ben didn't stay long because he was blowing so much, it he got all hot up there over Harlem. . .

that there was a great up there, Played saxophone player and the guys begin to go up and at the Rhythm listen. And then he would hang out down there with the Club, and, of course, I told Fletcher, I said, Fletcher, "You better snatch Ben up," so he did just that. And, of course -- then always like play, not fast -- he always like to play in a tempo that would show off his tone. He could play a beautiful ballad. Of course, he could swing to and play create some blues because he played -- besides playing saxophone, he always could play that funky F sharp piano, you know, I mean stride just like Meade Lux Lewis Meadlux louie and those guys, you know.
Man, he used to knock me out playing. He really

could play that stuff, you know. His only weakness -- well, before I say that -- he later wound up in Duke Ellington's band with the section along that "Cottontail" -- tuh-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta. Well, Ben wrote the reed chorus on that, I found out later, you know. Well, it sure moved. I know the bridge went -- da-da-da-da-duh-duttle-tee-duh, dee-deedle-deedle-duh-ba, deedle-deedle-deedle-dee-duh, deedle-deedle-deedle-duh, ba-deedle-deedle-deedle dee dum, one of those things. That was Ben Webster.

I didn't know that, but I got from an authentic source that Ben wrote that. But anyhow, he was great in that band, way, and he went to Europe with everybody. He had one fault, and he always thought he was a great gambler, not with the sharks of gambling, but I mean with the bands that he played, you know, he played cards. And he was always a bad loser. He always wanted to fight, man. This was when -- I found out those big cue ball eyes, when he would do them like that, he'd be mad.
